title: Immunity and vaccination

oak.lesson: Differences between infectious and non-infectious disease

oak.unit: Defences against pathogens, the human immune system and vaccination (KS4, for teacher background)

big_idea: White blood cells destroy pathogens, and memory cells mean the second attack by the same pathogen is beaten before you feel ill: that is immunity, and vaccines give it without the disease.
goals: I can describe how phagocytes and lymphocytes destroy microorganisms in the body.
I can explain why you only get many infectious diseases once, and how vaccination protects people and communities.

keywords.meaning: a blood cell that fights pathogens
a white blood cell that surrounds, ingests and digests microorganisms
a white blood cell that makes antibodies
a protein that sticks to one type of pathogen
fits only one type of pathogen
a lymphocyte that stays in the body ready to make antibodies quickly
protected against a disease, so you do not become ill with it
a substance containing parts of a pathogen, given to make a person immune
a very small pathogen that can only copy itself inside a cell
the amount of a medicine given at one time
the time for the amount of a medicine in the body to fall by half

misconceptions: Antibodies kill all pathogens in the same way. Each antibody is specific: it fits the surface of one type of pathogen, so immunity to measles gives no protection against chickenpox.

A vaccine gives you a mild case of the disease. A vaccine contains parts of a pathogen's surface (or a dead or weakened form) that cannot cause the disease, but still make lymphocytes produce antibodies and memory cells.
Antibiotics treat any infection. Antibiotics kill bacteria; they do nothing to viruses (this lesson's Think task and Lesson 4).

slides.subtitle: How does your body beat a pathogen, and how can a vaccine make you immune without the disease?
slides.notes: Lesson 2 of 9C. Last lesson: what causes disease. Today: what the body does about it, and how vaccines use the same system. The Challenge links to the Veterinary science STEM pages.

slides.title: Do Now: once is enough
prompt: Many people had chickenpox as a small child.
If a friend has it now, they will almost certainly not catch it again.
1. Suggest why you only get chickenpox once.
3. Name two things your body does to fight an infection.
slides.notes: Four minutes, in books. Do not confirm answers yet; collect ideas on the board (white blood cells, antibodies, 'the body remembers'). A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease. Q3: any sensible idea: white blood cells, raised temperature, skin as a barrier, coughing and sneezing.

slides.title: Today
slides.notes: Read each goal aloud. Point out the key words box on the worksheet. The Chinese key words version has the same words with Chinese beside them.

slides.title: Caught in the act
slides.question: This white blood cell (a phagocyte) is about to eat the bacteria next to it. What do you think happens next?
slides.caption: A phagocyte engulfing bacteria (electron micrograph, coloured)
text: Talk to a partner: what does your body do in the days after a pathogen gets in?
slides.notes: The phagocyte surrounds the bacteria, takes them inside itself (ingests them) and digests them with enzymes. Phagocytes work on any pathogen. The other kind of white blood cell, lymphocytes, are more particular, as we will see.

slides.title: Two kinds of white blood cell
slides.text: Your blood carries two main types of white blood cell that attack pathogens in different ways.
slides.key_idea: Phagocytes ingest pathogens. Lymphocytes make antibodies that fit the surface of one type of pathogen.
slides.notes: Left: a phagocyte surrounds and ingests a microorganism, then digests it. Right: a lymphocyte makes antibodies, proteins that stick to the outside of the pathogen. Antibodies can make pathogens burst, stick together in clumps, or be easier for phagocytes to ingest. Point out the memory cells box: we come back to it.

slides.title: Why you are ill before you get better
slides.caption: A lymphocyte (electron micrograph)
text: Each type of pathogen has a different surface, so it needs a different antibody.
Lymphocytes must make new, specific antibodies for each new pathogen.
This takes days. Meanwhile the pathogen multiplies and you feel ill.
Once there are enough antibodies, the pathogens are destroyed and you recover.
slides.key_idea: Antibodies are specific: each type fits only one type of pathogen.
slides.notes: Use a key and lock: one antibody fits one pathogen. Ask: if you are immune to measles, are you immune to chickenpox? No: different surface, different antibody needed. That is why a child can have measles and still get chickenpox.

slides.title: Memory cells make you immune
slides.text: After an infection, some lymphocytes stay in the body as memory cells.
slides.key_idea: The second time the same pathogen gets in, memory cells make antibodies fast and in large numbers: the pathogen is destroyed before you feel ill. You are immune.
slides.notes: Compare the two curves: the first response is slow and small, so you are ill for days. The second is fast and large, so the pathogen never gets a chance to multiply. This is why you only get measles once. Ask: where could a vaccine fit on this graph? (It gives the first response without the disease.)

slides.title: Vaccines
slides.caption: A vaccination
text: A vaccine contains parts of the surface coating of a pathogen (or a dead or weakened form).
Lymphocytes make antibodies and memory cells against it, without you having the disease.
If most people in a community are vaccinated, the pathogen cannot spread, which also protects people who cannot be vaccinated.
Viruses are not living: they can only copy themselves inside a cell.
slides.key_idea: Vaccination makes you immune without being ill.
slides.notes: The vaccine cannot cause the disease because it does not contain a working pathogen, but the surface parts are enough for lymphocytes to make the right antibody and memory cells. Community protection: a pathogen needs a chain of people to pass through; vaccinated people break the chain. Antibiotics do not work on viruses (Lesson 4).

slides.title: Quick check
slides.instruction: Mini whiteboards. One answer each, then we check.
questions: Which type of white blood cell ingests (eats) microorganisms?
Why do you only get measles once?
Does a measles vaccine protect you against chickenpox? Yes or no, and why.
slides.notes: Answers: phagocytes; antibodies (proteins that stick to pathogens); memory cells stay ready and make the right antibodies very quickly the second time, so you are immune; no, antibodies are specific and chickenpox has a different surface; parts of the pathogen's surface coating (or a dead or weakened pathogen).

slides.title: Your turn: fighting infection
steps: Core: complete the gap fill with the word bank, match the key words, then decide true or false.
Stretch: measles and chickenpox; how a vaccine protects a child; why viruses are not living.
Challenge: a vet's antibiotic dose. Use the half-life to work out when the ball python needs its next dose.
Finished? Answer the My thinking question about flu vaccines.
slides.footer: Use the words phagocyte, lymphocyte, antibody and memory cell correctly: they are not the same thing.
slides.notes: Half-life hint for Challenge: 10 mg/kg falls to 5 after one half-life (64 hours), then to 2.5 after two (128 hours). 128 hours is about 5.3 days, so a new dose is needed by day 5. Circulate and check the gap fill first.

slides.title: Protecting the whole community
slides.prompt: In a town, 95% of children are vaccinated against measles. The other 5% cannot be: some are babies, some are too ill. Why are those 5% also protected?
frames: Vaccinated people cannot ___, so the pathogen ___.
slides.notes: Expected: measles spreads from person to person; vaccinated people do not become ill or pass it on, so the chain of infection is broken and the virus rarely reaches an unvaccinated person. This only works when most people are vaccinated. Link to the polio story from Lesson 1.

slides.title: Exit ticket
questions: Name the two types of white blood cell and say what each one does.
Why do you only get measles once?
What does a vaccine contain, and why does it not give you the disease?
slides.notes: Answers: phagocytes ingest and digest microorganisms, lymphocytes make antibodies; memory cells remain after the first infection and make the specific antibodies very quickly next time; parts of the pathogen's surface coating (or a dead or weakened pathogen) that cannot cause the disease but still trigger antibodies and memory cells.

slides.title: What we learned
slides.next: Control systems: how nerves and hormones carry messages around the body, and why polio and chickenpox viruses attack nerve cells.
points: Phagocytes ingest and digest pathogens; lymphocytes make specific antibodies.
Making antibodies for a new pathogen takes days, which is why you are ill before you get better.
Memory cells make the second response fast and large: you are immune.
Vaccines contain parts of a pathogen and make you immune without the disease; vaccinating most of a community protects everyone.
slides.notes: Homework: Workbook pages 29 and 30 (9Ca Diseases; Veterinary science). The model of half-life on page 30 can be designed at home and tried in a later lesson if time allows.

worksheet.my_thinking: A flu vaccine has to be given every year, but one course of polio vaccine protects for life. What might be different about the flu virus?
exit: Name the two types of white blood cell and say what each one does.
Why do you only get measles once?
What does a vaccine contain, and why does it not give you the disease?

core: pathogen; Phagocytes, lymphocytes; antibodies; pathogen (or microorganisms), stick; ingested.

phagocyte: ingests and digests microorganisms; lymphocyte: makes antibodies; antibody: protein that sticks to one type of pathogen; memory cell: stays ready to make antibodies quickly; vaccine: contains parts of a pathogen and makes a person immune.
stretch: Secure answer: antibodies are specific. The measles virus and the chickenpox virus have different surfaces, so the antibodies and memory cells made against measles do not fit the chickenpox virus. Lymphocytes would have to make a new antibody from the start, so the child can still become ill with chickenpox.

Secure answer: the vaccine contains parts of the surface coating of the measles virus (or a weakened form) that cannot cause the disease. Lymphocytes make antibodies that fit the measles virus, and memory cells are formed. If the real virus later infects the child, the memory cells make large amounts of the right antibody very quickly, so the virus is destroyed before the child becomes ill.
Viruses cannot carry out life processes on their own: they do not respire, grow, feed or move, and they can only copy themselves (reproduce) inside a living cell.
challenge: a) The amount of medicine given at one time (here, in mg of antibiotic for each kg of the animal's mass). b) 10 mg/kg falls to 5 mg/kg after one half-life (64 hours) and to 2.5 mg/kg after two half-lives (128 hours). 128 hours = 5.3 days, so a second dose is needed by day 5 (accept 5 to 5.3 days). c) 15 mg/kg x 15 kg = 225 mg.

Secure answer: a pathogen spreads from one person to the next. Vaccinated people are immune, so they do not become ill and do not pass the pathogen on. When most people are vaccinated, the chain of infection is broken and the pathogen rarely reaches an unvaccinated person, so babies and ill people are protected as well. This only works if a high percentage of the community is vaccinated.
exit: Phagocytes ingest (surround and digest) microorganisms; lymphocytes make antibodies.
After the first infection, memory cells remain and make the specific antibodies very quickly and in large numbers the next time, so the virus is destroyed before you become ill (you are immune).
Parts of the pathogen's surface coating (or a dead or weakened pathogen); these cannot cause the disease but lymphocytes still make antibodies and memory cells against them.
answers.my_thinking: Open answer. Good answers suggest that the flu virus changes its surface coating from year to year, so last year's antibodies and memory cells no longer fit and a new vaccine is needed; the polio virus does not change in this way.
